name: Vibe Distribution
tagline: Distribute your product from the inside out.

source.summary: One AI SaaS ran the method for 97 days (Jun 2 – Sep 7, 2026): a free-tier app with a single $9 plan and a separate paid back-office suite on one platform; ~3,900 registered users and 174 paying accounts by the end; built by one founder with AI sessions. Numbers were reconstructed from the repository (2,244 commits, 486 merged PRs, 349 migrations), planning and audit documents, session notes and read-only production queries. 52 headline figures were adversarially re-verified: 17 confirmed as stated, 35 corrected to a narrower or later value, 0 refuted. Separately, 9 published conclusions were reversed by later data.
boundaries: Zero user interviews; every lesson is telemetry, tickets and transcripts.
Most funnel effects are comparisons, not randomized experiments.
Model quality was judge-scored, not human-scored.
Many cells are small (42 clickers, ~30 payers).
Costs beyond model spend and ads were never measured.
Organic and app-store channels were never measured.
No hiring or team scaling occurred; one founder with AI sessions ran every stage, so the journey has no hiring stage by design.
One product in one market: the laws generalize, the numbers are reference points.

confidence_labels.deploy: same product before and after a change
confidence_labels.measurement: the number changed because the counting was fixed, or it is a count with no counterfactual
confidence_labels.confounded: other changes landed in the same window
confidence_labels.replay: real past inputs re-run through the old and the new rule, before/after counted

metric_conventions.timezone: one named reporting timezone for every day boundary; never an offset
metric_conventions.core_request: a self-initiated action that produces the product's primary result; auto-generated and system-initiated results excluded
metric_conventions.day_zero: the reporting-timezone calendar day containing signup
metric_conventions.exclusions: internal accounts (any address on your domain and any browser ever signed in by staff), bot user agents at ingestion, today's partial day
metric_conventions.small_n: below 10 show counts; never quote a percentage with a numerator under 5 or a denominator under 100

voice: Track everything. And I mean EVERYTHING your users touch.

What moves the needle financially? Paid users? Credits? Then track downstream of those two or three core goals: what milestones does someone need to reach to hit those conversion events? Track each step to see where they're leaking out of your model.
what_the_data_said: Paid conversion by lifetime usage is a staircase: 0.6% for users with five or fewer requests, 5% at six to nineteen, 20% at twenty to forty-nine, 42% at fifty to ninety-nine, 78% past a hundred. Every milestone on that staircase is a thing to track.

Where they leaked: 13 of the 17 ad visitors who reached the paid suite's registration step never came back. On the free product the leak was one step, seeing the limit modal and not clicking it (23% click), because clicking it converted at 64%.
The first thing tracking showed was that the tracking was wrong: every signup read as “direct” because the attribution fields lived on a page nobody used.
209 audits in 97 days. Of 52 headline figures re-verified, 35 had to be narrowed or updated and nine published conclusions were reversed outright, each after it had changed a decision.
What users were not using: a meetings feature with 29 real uses in 90 days, a journal entry point 28 users had ever touched, a task system with 7 users. All cut in one day.

What users believed the product was: a deadline-driven tool (requests peak in the two days before a recurring deadline at more than twice the off-peak rate) whose most-typed topic was absent from every example prompt; and a general-purpose assistant, which became a mode.
$10,371 of spend bought 2,069 signups, ~278 activated users, and 79 payers at $131 each against ~$69 of gross lifetime value. Top-of-funnel was LTV-negative; only retargeting cleared.
The ad platform's cost per lead sat flat at $3.50–3.90 all summer while the cost of an activated user quadrupled.
Same creative, four audiences: 31% activation on the best, 12% on the worst. Audience beat creative; the “saturation” was a spend-rate problem.

The chat-native version of a back-office suite came with one law: whatever new interface you lead with, if it can be done by hand it must be doable there, no exceptions. 119 parity gaps were audited and the high ones closed the same day.

The differentiators nobody else built were found by research, not brainstorming: a migration that moves customers' stored payment credentials from the old vendor (no competitor did it), and the on-site rollout layer for the people who use the product every day, not just the buyer (“everyone trains the admin, nobody trains the person at the front desk”).
A competitor teardown run as dozens of parallel research sessions produced the gap matrix a two-day build ran against; the competitive read of the market leader ended “the moat is outward-facing”.

The cheapest win on record cost no ad spend: generating the first result before asking any setup question lifted day-zero activation from 4.9% to 8.7% (paid upgrades read 1.72 → 3.10 a day at first, but a later audit could not confirm the paid half).
Users who tried the product before signing up returned in week one at 1.8× the rate of cold signups, and made 2.8× the lifetime requests.

A UX audit run as 14 independent reviewer sessions scored the paid suite 6/10: “excellent rooms, broken hallways”. Showcase cards on its home drew 39 clicks against 289 on the sidebar across eight modules (0 vs 19 on the worst).
One setup field was filled in by 1 of 1,445 accounts; another was skipped by 28%. Setup was cut to two decisions and the first result now generates before any style question is asked.
Setup completed at 95% and still 38% of completers never used the product. The death point was the empty screen after setup, not setup.
295 things deleted in 97 days. A welcome page went from eleven blocks and eight animation loops to one card; a 971-line demo file and 48 sentences of feature copy went with it.

One option (“try it free”) on the front door: 27% of fresh visitors pressed it, and that rate held at 24–28% for nine weeks across four redesigns. Presentation never moved the door; the product behind it did the converting.
12.9% of fresh visitors signed up within seven days; most of those came straight from the front door, the rest after trying the product.

Conversion after the wow: try first, register at the moment you want to save, pay at the moment they hit the daily limit. Users who reach that limit pay at 28% versus 4% for matched users who never do.

$39 with a 30-day trial → 14-day trial → $29 with three struck-through anchors in five days → $9 a month, unlimited, no trial, everything free under six requests a day. Paying accounts then accumulated 79 → 174 over five weeks at a flat ~25 adds a week; the hard limit, not the price change, carries the conversion evidence.

Signups per week were flat at ~330 across the price cut. Daily-active free users then grew 54% between mid-July and late August while paid adds held at ~25 a week. The base grew; conversion per add did not.
Addiction first: conversion rises with lifetime use from under 1% to over 75%; churn is decided before the purchase by how many days someone used the free tier.

A plan-comparison table inside the limit modal was deleted: “those are for browsers; at the limit they were the scroll between the moment and the CTA.” The first hit is a single-CTA pitch; two in three who click it pay within 24 hours.
A hardcoded “Trusted by 340” lasted six days; a live count replaced it, and later a rounded count with a plus sign was replaced by the exact figure refreshed every five minutes.
A review reward works, but only asked in-app after value: users asked on day zero upgraded at 0%; users asked on day one or later, at 22%.
14.3% of paying users with zero or one free active day churned inside two weeks, versus 0 of 51 with four or more.
What happened before one user quit: he typed “continue” twelve times in seventy minutes and left 21 thumbs-up, 0 thumbs-down and 0 tickets. Every channel said he was happy.

Change they did not like: an editor overlay that fixed a real problem but appeared on every turn was reverted in ten hours. Simplification they did like: asking for feedback only after finished work interrupted 28% fewer people and lifted positive ratings from 30% to 34%.
The revenue model that compounded was 1.7× high within 26 days. The one that held is a line: flat intake × a retention plateau. Churn was assumed at 7% and measured at 13%.

Predictable for the customer: anything they must rely on (numbering, dates, prices, record writes) became deterministic code with the model as fallback, after a stored preference was ignored ten times.

What it cost to know: the audits were AI sessions reading production tables, transcripts and click streams. Their yield was a dozen silent outages found by audit and none by ticket. Budget for the reading: model spend for the whole product, audits included, was $245 in its busiest month, less than one week of the ad budget it corrected. Put the audit cost beside the ad line and compare.

punch_list: Sell the end result, not the features.
Make it as easy as possible. If it takes more than five clicks to sign up or pay, shorten it.
Don't give them too much to consume before they pay. Too much info = confusion = they leave.
Make it exciting. Make them want the end result even while using the product.
Even when they're already using the product, you're still selling them the dream, the outcome.
manifesto.closer: Less thinking. Fewer clicks. More excitement.

principles.title: Instrument every touch on day one, then spend the first month fixing the instruments
principles.voice: Track everything. And I mean EVERYTHING your users touch.
principles.why: You cannot optimize what you cannot see, and the first thing tracking shows you is that your tracking is wrong. The product this guide draws on shipped a behavioral ledger nine days after its first commit and then spent three months making every counter honest. Tracking is a product surface with its own bug class; the definitional rules matter more than the dashboards.

moves.text: Log every page view and click with a stable anonymous id before signup, plus explicit events for modals, sends, subscriptions and every surface where money or activation happens.
Name your two or three money events (paid conversion, credits, retention) and track every milestone downstream of them, so the leak has a step name.
Put attribution and conversion events on the surface real users touch, and fire them on the completed behavior (first message sent), never on the button click.
Write one internal-account rule and apply it in every counter and both data layers; a browser that has ever been signed in by staff is internal forever.
Drop bots at ingestion with the same detector you use at read time; clamp client clocks to server time; never trust a client's completion claim.
Give every surface an impression event from day one so conversion has a denominator, and give every offer surface its own event name with exactly one emitter.
Record the system's own decisions on the row (which model, which variant, degraded or not) so failures become a query instead of an inference.

evidence.text: Paid conversion by lifetime usage turned out to be a staircase, 0.6% → 5% → 20% → 42% → 78% across five usage bands. That staircase became the product's activation model, and it only exists because requests were counted per user from the start.

The leak in the free product was one step: 182 accounts saw the usage limit, 42 clicked it, 27 paid within 24 hours of the click. Naming the impression separately from the click is what made the 23% click rate visible.
The first audit found every signup labeled “direct” because the attribution fields were on a page nobody used. Ads had been running for weeks.
A preloaded payment form logged a “card started” event and triggered an abandoned-cart email to 182 people, 178 of whom had never touched a card field. One event name for two behaviors.

donts: Count any telemetry touch as “active”. Loading a page is not usage.
Sum money or cohorts from unpaged row pulls in application code.
Share one event name across two behaviors and then try to attribute.
Report a “usage drop” from a chart whose last bar is today.
principles.how_to_measure: Every headline total is a database function; page anything that could exceed your API layer's row cap (one popular one silently returns 1,000 rows and no error); cross-check any script's population against an exact count before it acts. Reset your reporting epoch to the minute the last event went live, name the timezone, and label backfilled rows forever.

principles.title: Make audits the operating system, on a cadence, with a hostile second reader
principles.voice: Audit everything on a weekly or biweekly basis. What are they using? What are they NOT using?
principles.why: An audit is not an event; it is the rhythm. Of 52 headline figures in this guide that were re-verified against their sources, 35 had to be narrowed or updated and nine published conclusions were reversed outright. Run one every few days on a rotating surface (feedback, funnel, billing, email, ads, model quality, copy accuracy), write each one as a hand-off with counts and reproduction queries, and have every decision-critical number re-derived by someone whose job is to prove it wrong. The signature of a working audit practice is the reversal: findings you published and later retracted by name.

moves.text: Schedule audits weekly or biweekly per surface and rank every element by reach × second-day return (reach = distinct users who saw the element in 90 days; second-day return = the share of them who came back the next day; rank by the product).
Write each audit as a hand-off: symptom, evidence with counts and the query, root cause at file and line, fix, verification, and “already fixed, do not redo”.
Re-derive every decision-critical claim independently before acting on it. Default a refuter to “refuted” when uncertain; fewer than two verdicts means unreviewed.
Measure blast radius in production before writing the fix; replay any classifier or routing rule against the full production corpus and pin the cases that broke as tests.
Keep a “corrections to the record” section in every plan revision so nobody reuses a retracted number.
End every audit in a persistent note with the numbers, the trap and the rule, so the next person inherits the measurement instead of re-running it.

evidence.text: 209 audits in 97 days. Five feedback audits in the first fourteen days of real traffic each fixed the top cause of negative ratings: a token cap, a greedy routing rule, refusal text spliced onto good output. “Model quality” was never the cause.
Adversarial review found 7 to 36 real defects per pass and kept finding defects in the fixes: one payments feature went 18 → 11 → 13 → 7 findings across four rounds before shipping.

The cut list from a 90-day usage audit removed a meetings feature (29 real uses), a journal entry point (28 users ever), a task system (7 users) and 64 zero-signal emails in one day, at no measured cost to daily actives.
A review workflow that lost most of its verifiers to a session limit silently marked 48 findings “refuted”, including a blocker. Hence the rule: no verdict is not a verdict.

donts: Accept a verdict handed to you instead of reading the row.
Re-run a query with a different window to get a better-looking number.
Read a regex instead of running it against real traffic.
Declare a feature done without checking that its consumer (a schedule, a caller) exists.
principles.how_to_measure: Count audits per week, reversals per month, and defects found per review pass. A healthy practice produces reversals; a practice with none is not auditing, it is confirming.

principles.title: The denominator is the most dangerous lever in your product
principles.voice: Your denominator is lying to you. One window, one cohort, one complete day. If the number moved, prove the counting didn't before you touch the product.
principles.why: Almost every scare in the record was a measurement artifact. A blended rate fell because the user base aged. A seven-day rate was window noise. An open rate was really a click rate. A churn tile counted trials that never paid. A “regression” came from a stuffed denominator. The honest read is per-tenure, per-cohort, pooled over thirty days, on one complete local day, keyed to money facts recorded when they happened.

moves.text: Stop managing to the blend; track per-tenure rates. Any metric with “all users ever” in the denominator falls mechanically as the base ages.
Cohort by first-seen; count a cohort only once its window has closed; fade immature days.
Drop today from every daily series. Score one complete local day, never a rolling 24 hours. Pool totals; never average daily percentages. Key rates off thirty days when you have ~25 events a week.
Funnel percentages are of the step above; one person ranks once; below n=10 show counts; never quote a percentage with a numerator under 5 or a denominator under 100.
Record money facts when they happen: paying means a subscription exists, first-paid is stamped by a trigger, churn is churned-paid over everyone who could have left, resubscribers are not churn.
Hold composition constant before calling a step change a regression; compare the same weekday and hour.
Causal claims come only from recorded holdout arms. A “success after send” is coincidence until a control says otherwise.

evidence.text: “Engaged weekly actives are falling” (27.9% → 25.9%) was the base aging: per-tenure engagement had risen at both ends, 48.8% → 63.1% for week-one users. Stop managing to the blend.
Trailing-7 and calendar-week conversion told opposite stories on the same data (2.04 → 1.41% vs 1.48 → 1.80%). Neither was real; the 30-day pooled rate had not moved.

Every dashboard “open rate” had been a click rate for ten days of a rewrite decision, because no open webhook was ever registered. True opens were about 45%, and the rewrite had cost about four points (45% → 39% at first read, 47.7% vs 44.0% once late opens landed) that the broken metric hid.
A churn tile read 20 when only 6 had ever paid; a start-of-month denominator would have reported 150% churn in a month that opened with 2 payers and added 63.
A “retention hole” for users who tried before signing up (18.5%) was an artifact of a skip event. Measured properly, those users retained better at every depth.

donts: Compound a base fed by flat intake and a plateaued retention curve.
Steer by a denominator the product itself moves (an auto-demo that manufactures one-message “chatters”).
Trust a status string or an event name over the money.
Lock an A/B winner on zero opens: “no open data” and “every candidate scored zero” look identical in the counts.
principles.how_to_measure: Two numerators over one denominator on every retention chart (touched vs used), so inflation cannot silently return. Detect batch backfills by shape (many rows sharing one timestamp) rather than by date. A failed read renders “unknown”, never a fake zero, and a caveat that switches itself off below a threshold is a bug.

principles.title: Find what nobody is building, then reach parity in your new interface for the rest
principles.voice: If all you do is duplicate what someone else did and offer it cheaper, shove your SaaS in the trash. You can build things in five minutes, so spend fifteen asking AI to research.
principles.why: In the AI age there are twelve products like yours. Differentiation comes from two places: the thing the incumbents structurally cannot do, and the thing users have been asking for in public for years that nobody built. Both are found by research, not brainstorming, and research is now cheaper than building.

moves.text: Before building any new surface, run a competitor teardown into a graded matrix: table stakes, important, differentiator, and an explicit “where we already lead, do not regress” list.
Read the public complaints (forums, review sites, help centers) for what people wish the incumbents did; grade the wishes by how often and how angrily they recur.

Pick the one capability the incumbents cannot copy without changing their business (moving customers' stored credentials, doing the physical rollout, running on the customer's own data) and make it the headline.

For everything else, lead with your new interface (chat, voice, automation, API, mobile) under one law: if it can be done by hand, it must be doable through the new interface, no exceptions. Audit parity as a list of gaps with file and line.
Look for where the category leader is polished inward (back office, admin tooling) and thin outward (what its customers' own users see); that gap is the headline.
Time-box research to a multiple of build time; a two-day build deserves a day of research.

evidence.text: The paid suite's positioning came from a competitor teardown, run as dozens of parallel research sessions, that found exactly one wholly missing table-stakes feature and a list of net-new concepts nobody had. The build ran against that matrix in two days.

The headline differentiator, migrating customers' stored payment credentials from the old vendor, was chosen because research showed no competitor did it. The on-site rollout layer was chosen because “everyone trains the admin, nobody trains the person at the front desk”.
The chat-parity audit found 119 gaps (21 high, 51 medium, 47 low); the high ones closed the same day.
The competitive read of the category's largest player ended: it had agents, voice and tooling, and “nothing outward-facing. Close the in-office polish gaps; the moat is outward-facing.”

donts: Chase a competitor's feature list instead of the gap they cannot cover.
Ship a mode that is a mock (“offering it promises a capability that isn't there”).
Collect credentials for integrations nothing consumes: 23 catalog entries were doing exactly that.
principles.how_to_measure: Adoption of a differentiator is counted by a durable row (a subscription, a completed migration), never by a page view. The suite in this record learned it had zero real users of its differentiator weeks after launch because it had been counting the wrong table.

principles.title: Experience is the cheapest conversion lever you have
principles.voice: It doesn't matter if your product is better at what it spits out. A good experience and a clean, easy interface is what keeps people coming back and referring their friends. It is the number one under-utilized optimization in the vibe-coding SaaS space, and the cheapest.
principles.why: Competitors with more money can buy their way past a worse result. They cannot buy the return visit. The largest single effect in this record came from a change that cost nothing to run: the first result generated before the user was asked anything.

moves.text: Make the first session end in a real result, not a success toast, an empty screen, or a tour.
Let people use the product before they create an account; gate the save, not the value.
One noun, one door: each concept gets one entry point; chrome appears only when it can act.
Cards, never modals; open the heavy workspace only on explicit navigation; live controls belong only to the newest item, older ones are read-only history.
Screenshot at phone width on a production build before shipping any change to a front door. In this record three in four signups were on a phone.
Read your own audit as “rooms and hallways”: module interiors can be excellent while the connective tissue reads as two products stapled together.

evidence.text: First-result-before-questions: day-zero activation 4.9% → 8.7% with zero ad spend. Paid upgrades read 1.72 → 3.10 a day at twelve days, but a later audit found 7-day paid conversion flat for accounts whose first result was auto-generated (2.4% vs 6.3% for those who skipped it), so treat the paid half as unverified.
Try-before-signup: users who used the whole free allowance returned in week one at 47.8% versus 26.1% for cold signups, and made 2.8× the lifetime requests.

Rooms and hallways: the paid suite scored 6/10 in an audit run as 14 independent reviewer sessions; its showcase cards drew 39 clicks against 289 on the sidebar across eight modules (0 vs 19 on the worst).
Two home surfaces giving different “first steps” was the core confusion; the fix was one setup resolver every surface derives from. “In an effort for simplicity we made this more complicated.”

donts: Two competing suggestion systems on the empty screen.
A tour authored on desktop landing on top of its own targets on phones.
Modules as cages (“I'm in this module so I can't do that”); one router handles every action from anywhere in the product, using the open module only as a hint.
principles.how_to_measure: Define activation as a small count of real actions in the first session (here: three requests and one save), measure week-one return by day-zero depth, and watch the ratio between users who complete setup and users who do anything after it.

principles.title: Simplify the first hour, not the product
principles.voice: Delete unnecessary questions. Save heavy inputs for later. Your goal is the shortest, cleanest, easiest route to the WOW moment. DELETE DELETE DELETE.
principles.why: Setup is almost never the leak. In this record 95% of users completed it and 38% of those never did anything afterwards. The death point was the empty screen after setup. Every pre-result question is a chance to stall in exactly that zone; every question after the first result is another engaged action.

moves.text: Infer what you can from what they bring (their files, their site, their history) and ask only what you must. Move every style, tone and length question to after the first result.
Never end setup, a connection or a success toast on an empty screen; the connection immediately does something with what was just connected.
One setup flow is the only setup script; the next step is deterministic; every surface (chat, cards, checklist, emails, admin) derives from one resolver.

Suggested starting points (chips, templates, example prompts, quick actions) come from what people organically do first, not from what you imagined; a pressed suggestion carries its intent and starts the action, it never just navigates.
Record writes execute immediately; only sends, bulk operations and money keep a confirm tap.
Zero interruptions: no tour on first load, no auto-starting guide, no modal between the user and the thing they were doing.
If signup or payment takes more than five clicks, shorten it: register and start paying in one modal; charge before creating the subscription so a declined card fails fast.

evidence.text: Fields nobody fills: one setup field was completed by 1 of 1,445 accounts, another skipped by 28%, a third filled by 16.5%. Setup was cut to two decisions.
Guided flows only complete when they start from a result: a “first win” flow started from nothing completed 3.4%; the same mechanic starting from an existing draft completed 47%.
Example prompts re-ranked from what people typed: the most-typed topic had been absent from every chip, and the most prominent chip ranked eleventh.

Interruptions: an auto-starting guide that opened when a user connected an account hijacked people mid-flow and was reverted in 84 minutes; a product tour was paused the day it was built and never earned its way back.
A pick-a-question step was removed from a generate flow: “choose a source, press write. That's the whole flow.” Net −495 lines.

donts: Collect preferences (style, tone, length, format, goals) before the first result; it engineers a one-perfect-output, one-and-done session (55% of requesters were already one-and-done).
Propose-then-confirm on every write; it made the assisted path slower than the form it replaced.
Two card systems on one screen; launcher chips that navigate.
principles.how_to_measure: Fill rate per setup field (delete anything under 20%); time to first request (three in four activators here sent within an hour of signup); share of setup completers with zero requests; clicks from landing to first result.

principles.title: Every sentence in the product is a claim; treat it like code
principles.voice: Simplify everything about the pitch. Sell the end result, not the features. And never let the product say something that isn't true.
principles.why: The most common defect in the record was not a broken mechanism but “code telling the user something untrue”: an import rendered as complete when it was cut, a label naming data that was not served, an email promising a trial that no longer existed, a landing page quoting a monthly allowance beside a daily limit. So copy got the treatment code gets: guards that read the source, tests that pin identical copy across surfaces, prices from one constant, and help text that must change before the behavior does.

moves.text: Write the one sentence first. If the value proposition needs a second sentence, the positioning is not done.
Every claim must be true at the moment it fires, for the trigger that fires it. When the product changes, rewrite the message; never let a message describe a product you no longer have.
Prices, limits and windows come from one constant shared by the landing, pricing, checkout, emails and help; a test bans literal dollars on public pages.
If any assistant or support bot answers from your documentation, that documentation is a build artifact: update it first, in the same change, and gate it in CI.
Never badge a fallback as the thing requested; omit a section with no data source rather than invent a number. No strip beats a lying strip.
Name the product, never the feature; retire abstract nouns for concrete outcomes; name the destination and stop, never describe where a control sits.
Names are data: replies come from the company, not a founder's name, once a machine drafts them; internal words (“agent”) never reach the customer.
Rename to what the customer says (“Go live”, not “Implementation”).
Verify copy on the rendered page and in screenshots, never in the editor; run copy guards against comment-stripped source.

evidence.text: A machine check of the help text (643 quoted strings, 90 numbers, 52 navigation paths) found 12 wrong claims; four told a free user to pay for something they already had.

A support reply grounded in a help section was bound to that section's content hash; editing the section retired every pending reply. One draft had told a user a thing could not be changed 101 minutes before the feature shipped.
About a thousand accounts were shown a label for data that was not what they were served: “re-fetching costs a request; mislabeling costs trust”.
Subject lines containing the product name opened 9–12 points lower in the same cohort; a question and the recipient's own context won.
The trial was removed by decision and still promised in the highest-intent emails three weeks later; a stale price survived two price changes in scripts nobody reread.

A rounded “+” user count lasted a day; the exact live count, refreshed every five minutes, stayed. A landing page still quoted a monthly allowance beside a published daily limit at the time of writing: the guide's own unresolved contradiction.

donts: Sell an implementation detail as the hook (“nothing sends until you say so”).
“Oh, and it's free”: one feature reading as the free thing.
Name five competitors in a switching strip; it tells the sixth it isn't about them.
Announce candor (“I'd rather tell you plainly…”); it is the same answer wearing a hat.
principles.how_to_measure: Share of public claims machine-checked against code; wrong claims found per copy audit; copy drift between surfaces caught by tests that pin identical strings; support replies invalidated by a help edit.

principles.title: One sentence, one option, and the door is the product
principles.voice: Can you explain your entire value proposition in one sentence? No? Then you don't understand your customer or your product. Do NOT list features. Tease the wow moment, then give them one option: see it.
principles.why: The front door in this record was rebuilt four times in nine weeks and its click-through never moved. What converted was what happened after the click. A landing page's job is to get the visitor into the product with the least possible thinking; the product's job is the rest.

moves.text: Write the one sentence first; if it needs a second, the positioning is not done.
One primary action, and it is the product itself (“try it free”), not a demo video, not a features tour.
Show the product, not motion: still frames drawn from the product's real geometry beat looping animations.
Reviews and the badge above the fold; the user count exact and live, never rounded, never with a plus sign.
The root domain is the landing and never redirects; a signed-in visitor gets their app in place.
Every dollar and limit on the page comes from one constant shared with pricing and the product, so copy cannot drift from what is enforced.

Treat any change to a front door as an experiment with signups per fresh visitor within seven days as the metric. A door that leaks 56% but produces ~900 direct signups a month cannot be judged by the leak alone.

evidence.text: Front-door click-through held at 24–28% across four redesigns, a demo added and removed, a cross-link removed and a copy change. “Presentation never moved it.”
10,098 fresh visitors in a month: 27% pressed the one option, 16% finished the one setup step, 11% sent something of their own, 12.9% created an account within seven days.
The paid suite's welcome went from eleven blocks and eight animation loops to one card and a real composer; a fake composer had drifted from the price and the promise.
A cross-link from the free product's welcome into the paid suite was removed as “an exit sign on the front door”; each product is reached by its own URL and never advertised at from inside the other.

donts: List features; forty-eight sentences of them were replaced by chips and then the chips were cut too.
Name five competitors in a switching strip; it tells the sixth it isn't about them.
Ship a copy contradiction between the page and the product (a monthly allowance on the landing beside a published daily cap).
principles.how_to_measure: Fresh visitors per day (dedupe by browser id, drop bots at ingestion), primary-action rate, signups within seven days per fresh visitor, and the share of visitors who leave with no tracked action. Instrument the door before you redesign it; in this record no pre-door era existed to compare against.

principles.title: Robots.txt is not evidence of access
principles.voice: If a crawler can't reach the page, nothing else about SEO matters. Verify with the crawler's own identity or you're guessing.
principles.why: A 240-article blog in eight days was the first growth engine in the record, and then it went quiet. What lasted was the hygiene: the root domain as the entry that never redirects, public pages that are actually public, structured data that asserts only what the code can source. The humbling finding came late: every AI crawler had been blocked at the CDN edge for months while robots.txt said allowed, and the visibility score everyone had been reading was measured through the block. Yield was never measured; the blog's view counter is zero on every row.

moves.text: After any public-page or CDN change, fetch every public path as each crawler (its own user agent) and check the status; purge the CDN first. Any measurement taken while blocked is invalid.
Adding a public page is a two-file change: the route and the auth allowlist. Never list a redirect beside its target in the sitemap.
The root domain is canonical and never redirects. A signed-in visitor gets the app in place; everyone else gets the landing and its structured data.
Structured data asserts only facts the code can source: Organization, WebSite, SoftwareApplication. No physical-business schema for a web product; no aggregate rating from third-party reviews.
Links exist as real anchors in server-rendered HTML; freshness derives from real edits only, never backdated.
Prerender content at build time with the environment present, so crawler load does not render pages on demand.
Fix content hygiene corpus-wide from an auditor's failing checks: image formats, title length, alt text, one H1, internal links.
Guest posts and satellite content are value-first with natural in-content anchors; the generator prints, it never publishes.
Measure yield (referrer → signup by month, including AI answer engines) or say it is unmeasured.

evidence.text: 0 of 242 posts were prerendered because the build lacked environment variables; every article rendered on demand under crawler load and was the site-wide slowness root cause.
Every AI crawler received 403 at the edge until the day it was found; audits reading robots.txt had reported “allowed”. The score of 42/100 was a floor, not a measurement.
5 of 11 sitemap routes told crawlers to index and then redirected them to login; the bug class recurred at least five times because the auth allowlist was not part of “adding a page”.
Posts with in-content internal links went 37 → 244 after a deterministic related-reading ring; 11 thin articles were expanded.

AI answer engines delivered ~20 signups lifetime, by month 1 / 3 / 8 / 7, rising after the unblock. Blog-attributed signups: 35 since tags began. Four satellite domains with 181 posts were never traced to a single signup.

donts: Believe a page is crawlable because a modal only visually covers the link; crawlers parse the DOM.
Mark up third-party ratings on your own site.
Add trust headers to clear a browser password-reuse warning; only a review request clears it.
Publish hundreds of articles and never read a yield number.
principles.how_to_measure: HTTP status per public path per crawler user agent; indexable routes vs the auth allowlist (diff must be empty); signups by referrer and by AI engine per month; content pages that landed a visitor who later signed up.

principles.title: One price, no trial, and a free tier that is genuinely useful under a hard limit
principles.voice: Multiple package options are dead. Give them ONE option: volume or access. Trials are antiquated. You have to get users addicted first.
principles.why: The product in this record went from $39 with a trial to $9 unlimited with no trial and everything free under six requests a day. Every conversion number that followed was measured on that plan. The free tier does the selling; the paid plan removes the ceiling; the limit is published everywhere and never tested per customer.

moves.text: One paid plan that removes the ceiling; it does not gate features. If a second option costs you nothing extra to serve, it costs you a decision at the moment of purchase. This is the evidence for a usage-metered product with near-zero marginal cost per free user; if your value is per seat or per integration, the analogue is one plan per seat with the usage limit as the single upgrade trigger. Measure paid adds per week either way.
Kill the trial. Free is the trial, and it never expires; the limit is the pitch.
Publish the limit everywhere and never A/B it per customer; a published limit is a promise.
Charge before creating the subscription; exactly one checkout in flight per account; never re-charge an account with a live subscription.
Keep the exit open: cancel is never disabled or gated on an essay; the retention offer comes after the cancel, never instead of it; refund unused annual months automatically.
Add annual as a switch on the same plan, not a second package.

evidence.text: Paying accounts accumulated 79 → 174 over five weeks at a flat ~25 adds a week ($711 → ~$1,540 monthly recurring). The hard limit carries the conversion evidence; the effect of removing the trial and the anchors was never isolated. Measure your own trial removal against paid adds per week, not against the paying-account total.
Signups per week were flat at ~330 across the price cut; daily-active free users grew 54% afterwards while paid adds stayed flat. There is no pre-cut baseline at the old price.
Three struck-through anchors in five days were dropped so the price read as a flat number; no anchor was ever measured to help.
The trial was “dead by decision” and still promised in the highest-intent emails three weeks later; every mention had to be scrubbed and pinned by a test.
One of a user's free daily requests was consumed by an attempt that produced nothing; the rule became: charge the allowance on the delivered result, never on the attempt.

donts: A struck-through launch anchor and a countdown timer (added, shrunk, removed within days).
Counting comped accounts as revenue, or overloading the plan-status column with descriptive values (a custom status silently revoked access).
Letting the processor's “charge on next cycle” default give every new subscriber a silent free month.
principles.how_to_measure: Paid adds per week (the metric), the share of the base that ever reaches the limit (69% never did here), time from signup to first paid signal (median 0.7 days, 53% same day, flat after day seven), and first-paid stamped by a database trigger so cancellations cannot erase it.

principles.title: The block causes the purchase; make the moment clean
principles.voice: Limit details. Boil the benefits down to what matters most. The least amount of options is the easiest choice. Boil the paid version down to a single voice: do or don't, we'll survive either way.
principles.why: Users who hit the free limit paid at 28% against 4% for matched users who never did, and every softer substitute (emails opened or not, banners, modals shown to users below the limit) converted zero of 776. The limit works because of the value received before it, so never push it earlier; and it works best when nothing stands between the moment and the button.

moves.text: The first limit hit is a clean price pitch with a single CTA, written to convert, not to apologize. Show what they would lose (the work they were doing, blurred).
Nothing to scroll between the moment and the CTA: no plan comparison, no feature grid, no second offer.
Escape offers (a review reward, a bonus allowance) belong to the second hit day and later, never the first.
Pitch inside the decision window (week one) and demote after day seven; sequence offers by depth, not calendar.
Paywall at send, after they have invested (let them build the thing first, then show the price when they press send), never a cold paywall on a click.
A “someone just upgraded” widget beside the pitch, fed by real recent events; the exact user count; the review badge. One choice; more choices later.
Keep the exit open at the same standard: cancel is never disabled or gated on an essay; the retention offer comes after the cancel, never instead of it.

evidence.text: 28.0% vs 4.3% at matched lifetime usage; 20% of all limit-hitters upgraded, typically within minutes of the hit.
Click → pay at the limit modal 64% (27 of 42) vs 10% from the header; the leak was impression → click (23%), not click → pay.

A plan-comparison table inside the limit modal was deleted: “those are for browsers”. A cold paywall on a settings click converted ~0 of 57 viewers; pricing at send, after the user had typed the invite, replaced it.
A user clicked Cancel five times on a greyed-out button and stayed subscribed three weeks: “a user who cannot stop being charged is a much worse failure than a blank feedback field”.
Two goodbye emails 94 seconds apart and a retention offer standing between the user and the exit were both removed; a user only hears goodbye once.

donts: Push the limit earlier; it converts because of depth received.
Put a feature-comparison table inside the limit modal (“those are for browsers”).
Offer a free month to a user asking for a refund; ask money from someone who already pays.
principles.how_to_measure: Limit impressions and clicks as separate events with one emitter each; click → pay within 24 hours by surface, like for like; median minutes from last impression to payment for limit payers; cancel completion rate and time.

principles.title: Social proof is computed, curated and live; the review ask is timed, never mailed
principles.voice: Reviews, reviews, reviews. Get your mom, your dog and your brother to leave five-star reviews and add that badge. Then compute the rest live.
principles.why: The review ask is the most expensive sentence your product can say to the wrong person: asked on signup day it produced reviewers who never paid; asked after value it produced dozens of real reviews on a small reward. Lifetime claim totals turned out to be mostly backfill batches, a mandatory “proof” step verified nothing, and a routing decision quietly filled the wrong listing. Referral loops, meanwhile, produced exactly one invitation in two weeks: a loop needs intake to amplify.

moves.text: Compute counts live and exact: no plus sign, no rounding. Render a committed value first and swap to a cached live read; a stale exact number is the honest fallback.
Testimonials come from real in-app feedback curated in the database with a negative-sentiment net; never surface internal accounts.
Ask for reviews in-app only, after a real moment of value, on day one or later with real usage behind it, never by email and never during checkout.
Mood outranks history: never invite someone whose newest signal is negative.
Offer the reward to everyone asked; protect the paid funnel by timing, never by price. Make the reward something a paying user does not want (extra allowance, not a free month of the plan).
Route by what each review site accepts (business vs personal addresses) and hedge the remainder with a stable split, so a returning reviewer sees the same site.
Treat imported reviews as data: verbatim, first name and initial, four stars and up, the aggregate is the listing's own number.
A “someone just upgraded” widget shows real, recent, named-by-org events; the vote itself pays nothing.
Referral rewards pay on qualification (a real activated account), never on send; count the loop by durable rows, not impressions, and do not build it before intake exists.

evidence.text: Reviewers asked on day zero (45% of claims, averaging four requests) upgraded at 0%; reviewers asked on day one or later, at 22%.
Organic claims ran ~4 a week; the lifetime total of 68 was mostly three backfill batches. Filter minutes with four or more grants before quoting anything.
A mandatory proof screenshot was followed by claims falling from 41.7% (5 of 12) to 8.6%, and it was never even uploaded; four other changes landed in the same window.

Diverting every personal-address user to one review site filled it 35 to 6 in ten days while the team believed it had moved to the other; a 70/30 hedge replaced it and organic claims rose from ~3 to ~7 a week.
Two review sites at 4.9 and 4.8 stars after ~50 reviews; the badge and cards sit above the fold on the landing with the exact live user count.
A referral program built with a heavy review produced 1 invitation (the team's own test) and 13 impressions in two weeks; “no loop exists to produce compounding” when intake is flat.

donts: A free month of the paid plan as a review reward (“the most cannibalizing reward available”).
Withhold the reward from heavy users to protect upgrades: “a cheaper review is worth nothing if it costs a star”.
Compute a listing's rating from the subset you imported.
Pay referral rewards on send (“the panel is a vending machine”).
principles.how_to_measure: Ask impressions → click-outs → claims with batch minutes filtered; reviewer upgrade rate by day asked; click-outs by site vs intended split; referral invitations, qualifications and payouts as durable rows.

principles.title: Every feature carries a measurement and a decision rule
principles.voice: If fifty people saw it and nobody used it, it's gone. Ship the delete today.
principles.why: 295 things were removed, reverted, paused or deliberately not built in 97 days, many the same day they shipped. The decision rules were consistent: dead on data, dishonest to the user, a second door on one noun, a promise the product cannot keep, a duplicate of an in-app offer, or motion where a visitor wanted the product.

moves.text: Kill anything with fifty or more exposures and zero successes. Give unmeasurable things a success event or ship them inactive; never guess.
Kill any surface that presents a choice you cannot honor or a capability that does not exist.
Kill the second door. One noun, one entry point; the card is the door; chrome is earned by state.
Ship dark behind a flag with an environment-only kill switch, so a decision day is a config flip, not a deploy. A kill switch is a rollback, never a hide.
When a fix was right but too broad, revert whole and re-scope. When a kill removed a live consumer, restore it.
Delete rather than disable anything that must never fire again.
Simplify, but never kill an email or surface that measurably helps return; never regrow a program without a holdout.

evidence.text: “14 days of data settled it: the carousel drew 16 clicks from 9 users. Gone.”
Bonus-task chips in the limit modal: zero takers ever, and click-only instrumentation had hidden that nobody saw them.

The lifecycle email catalog went 170 → 77 active rows in one day (64 zero-signal, 23 folds, 15 unjudged pitches) at a measured cost of ~1.5% of daily-active days; every paid pitch by email was 0 of 274.

A data option with nothing behind it was serving 167 accounts something else; it was removed the day the audit found it. Twenty-three integration entries that collected credentials nothing consumed became “coming soon”.
An overlay that fixed a real problem but appeared on every turn was reverted in ten hours rather than patched: “the mistake was scope, not the idea.”

donts: Default a retired sender on, so it can resurrect beside its replacement.
Disable instead of delete a sender that must never fire.
Kill on a percentage of nothing, or on a claim later found false.
principles.how_to_measure: Rank every element by reach × second-day return over 90 days; sweep for surfaces with ≥50 exposures and 0 successes; for each candidate check its live consumers (an email may still send the link) before deleting the route.

principles.title: Churn is decided before the purchase
principles.voice: Why are they quitting? What happened before they quit? Users don't like change, but they do like simplification.
principles.why: Post-purchase nudges never got built because nothing post-purchase predicted churn. What predicted it was how many days a user had used the free product before paying. And the users who leave loudest in the data are silent everywhere else.

moves.text: Measure churn on exposure (cancels over account-months), not on a start-of-month base, and separate first-cycle churn from post-renewal churn.
Read churn by pre-pay tenure; walk users to the paywall on real value rather than pulling it forward.
Trace one churned user second by second before theorizing: the click stream, the retries, what they typed.
Read frustration from repeat clicks and typed retries, never from ratings alone.
Someone on the way out gets a question (“was anything confusing?”), not the offer again; put the answers verbatim above the charts.
Change the product by simplifying it; revert changes that add chrome, however well-intentioned.

evidence.text: Churn inside fourteen days: 14.3% for payers with 0–1 free active days vs 0 of 51 with four or more. Churned payers used the product more, not less; price was 1 of 19 stated reasons.

Measured churn 13% a month (75% of cancels inside the first billing cycle) against a 7% planning assumption; the assumption had survived because the model's own caveat switched itself off below a sample threshold.
A churned power user: 51,000 characters of clean output and 15,000 severed, eight minutes apart; “continue” typed twelve times; 21 thumbs-up, 0 thumbs-down, 0 tickets; cancelled after 15 days.
Asking “how'd we do?” only after finished work: 28% fewer interruptions, positive ratings 30% → 34%, 81% of reward claims retained.
A user clicked Cancel five times on a greyed-out button and stayed subscribed three weeks; the mandatory exit note was removed the day it was found.

donts: Build “use it more” nudges after the purchase.
Count cancel events as churn: four of eighteen were on live subscriptions, two of them re-buying the same afternoon to change a card.
Send two goodbye emails 94 seconds apart.
principles.how_to_measure: Cancels ÷ account-months with a confidence interval; churn-14 by pre-pay active days; first-cycle vs post-renewal; and the retention curve plotted from day one (day zero is the denominator, never a column).

principles.title: Steer on cost per activated user from your own database, never on the platform's cost per lead
principles.voice: Audit ads against revenue, usage and goal effectiveness.
principles.why: The ad platform's cost per lead sat flat all summer while the cost of a user who actually used the product quadrupled. Read from production by campaign tag, top-of-funnel was LTV-negative, audience beat creative, and “saturation” was a spend-rate problem, not a creative one.

moves.text: Join every ad to production by its campaign tag and steer on cost per activated user and cost per payer against gross lifetime value.
Rank audiences before creatives; hold creative constant across audiences to see the spread.
Scale by spend rate per audience, never by consolidating budget into the best one until it saturates.
Treat top-of-funnel as a usage buy until a payer clears LTV; fund only the retargeting that clears it; cut placements that yield zero activated users.
Write the ad as a concrete task, not positioning; never promise a door a signup cannot find.
Put the pixel on the pages the campaigns point at (here it was missing from the paid suite's landing, pricing and checkout for two months) and, if you host pages for your customers, never on those.
Schedule dated reads with kill rules and re-derive the scorecard with a skeptic before touching budgets.

evidence.text: $10,371 → 2,069 signups ($5.01) → ~278 activated users (~$37) → 79 payers ($131) against ~$69 gross LTV. Only retargeting ($52 a payer, 10.5% paying) cleared.
The best audience set: $5.00 a signup and 15–16% activation at $400–540 a week; $5.70–6.30 and 7–11% at $540–870 a week after the budget was consolidated into it.

Concrete-task copy 20.8% activation vs positioning copy 13.7%; the two “+ AI” visuals and the two brand-adjective visuals were the four worst performers. Buzzword and brand-adjective visuals lose to the task the user will actually do; write the ad as that task.
One placement family spent $115 for zero activated users and zero payers; another cost $438 per payer.

Ads bought clicks to the paid suite and, for weeks, delivered the people to the free product: registration redirected 1.3 seconds after signup. “The bug that cost us every lead we ever had.” Verify the ad's landing → signup → destination path as a real user before spending.

donts: Optimize on the platform's lead count (it overcounted signups by a third and hid a 4× cost rise).
Blame the creative for saturation you caused with spend.
Mount the pixel in a layout that also wraps customer sites.
principles.how_to_measure: Per ad: signups, activated users (a real-usage threshold in one day), payers, and dollars per each, joined by tag from your own tables. Never quote the platform's number for anything downstream of the click.

principles.title: Email retains; it does not activate or convert
principles.voice: Even when they're already using the product, you're still selling them the dream. But not by email.
principles.why: Lifecycle email opened at 48% and every holdout was flat. Emails that handed a user back their own unfinished work were followed by product activity 41–45% of the time (post-send activity, uncontrolled); emails trying to activate users who had never started, 1–3% despite similar opens. On the strict click-then-return read the best message managed 10 of 436 and every paid pitch 0 of 274. The engine that emerged is behavior-triggered, capped, idempotent, and judged only by recorded control groups.

moves.text: Success is the product action after the send, never the open. Every email deep-links to a specific object or flow, never the dashboard.

Claim an idempotent ledger key before calling the provider; one engine, never a second email system, so caps see every send. Every broadcast writes a ledger row with the provider id or it has no open rate.
Record 20% holdouts as ledger rows and cite only holdout deltas.
Global rules in the engine: local morning window, one lifecycle email a day, three or four a week, suppress on success or activity, pause after ten dormant days.
Never pitch money by email when the product already makes the offer; dunning is exempt from every pitch suppression.
Keep the product name out of subject lines; a question or the recipient's own context wins.
Push: spend the single deniable OS dialog only on a real value moment through a primer card; count reach as id + opted-in + token.
Broadcast scripts are dry-run by default, send one test copy with a flag, and never run on a partial audience.

evidence.text: Replacing a linear drip (zero measured successes, 1.6–1.8× duplicate sends; its dashboard's “1–3% opens” turned out to be a click rate, true opens were 45–58%) with a behavior-triggered engine and a claim-before-send ledger: exactly one send per trigger, and opens finally measured at 48%.
Holdouts: no detectable lift from any lifecycle email at 9–13-point detectable effects; the comeback email that was planned as a +7-point lever was re-sized to +1–3 and read flat.
Subject lines with the product name opened 9–12 points lower in the same cohort; a question form and the recipient's own context won.
A text message saying “your allowance is back” brought 66% of recipients back: the best-performing message in the system, because it announced a product state.
Push never became a channel: a cold permission dialog was denied 41 times to 39 grants; 35 “reachable” devices were 6; 0 of 251 returns came from push.

donts: Spend more on activation copywriting when opens are already 30–40%; the constraint is payload, not subject lines.
Lock a subject-line winner on zero opens (9,110 sends went out under the wrong subject).
Let a broadcast outside the engine silence the engine's caps the next day.
Point reply-to at a personal mailbox; a reply sat unread in spam for a week.
principles.how_to_measure: Click-then-return per message, holdout delta per message, opens as context only. “Failed” means the provider failed; a suppression is “skipped” (505 of 507 “failed” rows in one month were skips).

principles.title: Fewer clicks includes the ones spent waiting
principles.voice: If the page is slow, the click didn't happen. Speed is UX, and it is the part of UX competitors can't see you fix.
principles.why: The record's speed wins were not micro-optimizations. They were structural: totals computed in the database instead of the app, the slowest dependency called directly instead of through a middle layer, common intents handled in code before any model runs, content prerendered at build. Each moved a customer-facing number by a multiple, and each was found by measuring under real load rather than alone.

moves.text: Aggregate in the database from day one; a table's volume being near zero today is exactly how you talk yourself into the slow shape.
Measure under concurrency. Solo timings lie; the burst is the failure. Gate heavy reads, dedupe in-flight requests, never cache a degraded read.
Benchmark the one call on the critical path direct vs through a proxy; call your slowest dependency directly.
Handle the predictable intents in code before any probabilistic component runs: pricing questions, common record writes, formatting.
Code-split the surfaces nobody opens on first load; prerender content at build with the environment present.
Stream anything that can exceed the proxy ceiling (~100 seconds on a common CDN) with heartbeats; give per-file work a wall-clock budget so a batch finishes in one run.
Preconnect to cold third-party hosts on the checkout path and record time-to-interactive for the payment form daily.

evidence.text: A dashboard query 40.8s → 1.03s (it had never once completed under an 8s timeout); a refresh job 17–22s every ten minutes → ~0.7s by recomputing only the ~7 users who changed instead of all 3,568.
The assistant's answer 15.3s → 2.4s per prompt and first byte 5–7s → 0.5–0.7s by moving the call onto a direct connection; a comparable call through a proxy was 17× slower.
Record writes parsed deterministically: 6–11 seconds with 3 of 6 silently dropped → ~1.7 seconds with none dropped. Pricing questions: ~10 seconds and two model calls → zero model calls.

The largest client bundle 776 KB → 328 KB by splitting five rarely-opened surfaces; a cold overview page 3.3s → 0.75s by removing an unconditionally awaited vendor probe and four serial profile reads.

A payment form took 3.1–4.1 seconds to become interactive every day for two weeks because two cold third-party hosts waited on one call; 8 of 14 bulk imports were cut at exactly 125 seconds by the proxy while every file had landed.

donts: Trust a timing measured alone on a quiet database.
Stream the whole event table into application code three times per cache miss.
Let a middle layer sit between you and the slowest call on the critical path without measuring it.
principles.how_to_measure: p50 and p95 per critical call under real load; time to first byte of the core result; share of long requests cut by the proxy ceiling; payment-form time-to-interactive per day.

principles.title: Nobody will tell you; run reliability like a growth channel
principles.voice: Zero interruptions. None of it survives an answer that dies mid-sentence.
principles.why: Ten days in which 6% of all output was saved cut off mid-sentence produced zero support tickets. Four days of zero grounded answers at HTTP 200 produced zero tickets. Three double-charged accounts produced one complaint. Users retry silently and then leave, and their judgment that the product got worse outlives the outage.
principles.moves_lead: Every third-party dependency (AI model, payments, maps, email, search) gets the same treatment: monitor the output property, not the vendor's status; persist the result before delivering it; set fallback deadlines from the fallback's own latency.

moves.text: Run a daily read-only health check on one complete local day with backtested thresholds and a decision table, and report every day including quiet days. 0.00% is not good news.

Key every canary on a field written unconditionally (which path served it, whether the fallback served it, whether the result was complete and used the data it should have), never on the absence of an optional flag.
Persist the answer before any second model call or stream write; a disconnect stops writing to the client, not finishing the work.
Detect a stalled provider by silence on the first byte; set the deadline from the fallback's latency distribution and well above the primary's p99; trip on two stalls, not one.
Register every streaming route with the shutdown drain; batch deploys; stream anything that can exceed the proxy ceiling (~100 seconds on a common CDN).
Aggregate in the database from day one; gate heavy dashboard reads; never cache a degraded payload. Solo timings lie; the burst is the failure.
Fail closed where a wrong “yes” costs money or data; fail open where a read blip would lock out paying users; write both directions down.
Any cron route ships with its schedule and a coverage test; a consumer without a producer changes nothing.

evidence.text: 493 answers severed over ten days (~49 a day, 196 accounts), 88.6% ending mid-word; found by accident while checking something else. A daily check with a backtested page rule (5 true positives, 0 false alarms) followed.

Retrieval died for 4 days 5.5 hours because an embeddings account ran out of credit; the app returned 200 with fluent, ungrounded answers. The only canary that would have caught it is the grounded-answer rate. The general form: for any dependency that can fail silently, the canary is a property of the output (did the answer use the data, did the payment settle, did the map render), never the dependency's HTTP status.
23 deploys in 17 hours cut 68 streams, 56% of all failures inside 15 minutes of a deploy; only one route family had registered with the drain.
Eight dashboard queries at 1–2 seconds each all crossed an 8-second timeout together whenever a deploy fired them at once, and zeros were then cached for two minutes.
A billing-anomaly job shipped without a schedule and never ran once while reported as working; a function redefinition silently dropped a security property and took signups down 3.5 hours.

donts: Use real user requests as recovery probes (loss stayed at 17–40%).
Alert nightly on a standing problem; it gets muted, and the one that mattered is muted with it.
Trust the repo's cron definitions or env defaults as evidence of what production is doing.
principles.how_to_measure: Broken-output share per day per surface with a volume gate; degraded share per day; grounded-answer rate per hour; stream failures within 15 minutes of a deploy; ledger vs processor reconciliation nightly, deduped by fingerprint so silence means clean.

principles.title: Support is a bug-report pipeline that replies as a consequence
principles.voice: Every ticket is a bug report. Fix the bug, verify the fix, THEN reply. Nobody wants a conversation; they want it to work.
principles.why: Whether a person or an agent works the queue, the pipeline is the same. Every support message, feedback form and negative rating becomes a job. An engineer or a coding agent fixes the bug in a throwaway branch, a hostile second read merges or holds it, the deploy is verified against that report, and only then does “it's fixed, try again” go out. The laws are about asymmetry: a wrong “no” costs one glance at a panel; a wrong “yes” costs a user their problem.

moves.text: Mirror every support message, form and thumbs-down into a jobs queue; the database row is the queue.
Fix bugs, never build features from the queue; a feature need pauses whoever is working the queue and pages a human.
“Fixed” means merged and serving and independently verified against that report; money, auth and core paths never merge unattended.
Reply only into a thread the user opened; a tapped chip is not a message; a ticket needs an account so a reply has somewhere to land.
Tone: thank, confirm fixed, ask them to try again; five sentences at most; never explain your cause; never name another customer.
Deny by default with named refusals recorded on the job; the kill switch is a database row read fresh on every send.
Classify the ticket first: one in five “support” tickets here were people trying to use the product through the support box.
Run daily scans for the things nobody writes in about (billing ledger, degraded share, stranded drafts).

evidence.text: Before the safety work: 60 of 64 agent runs were blind to the thread, a wording-based gate released 1 of 54 drafts, and two readings of the same 54 drafts disagreed 2 vs 24. The gate had made the founder the support team.
A rule that refused stale drafts and did nothing else left five users waiting 62–95 hours behind an empty-looking queue: “a rule that quietly removes people from the queue is worse than no rule.”
One held draft was retried 5,749 times because a money-rule regex matched a feature name. “A hold that survives the merge is a decision, not a delay.”
Three double-charged accounts, one complaint; a nightly ledger reconcile now finds what users do not report.

donts: Keyword-classify the ticket to decide autonomy; a churn threat landed in the how-to bucket.
Gate the reply on the merge rather than on the deploy serving the fix.
Give an unattended process the whole inbox.
principles.how_to_measure: Jobs by verdict (sent, held, refused) and by lane (how-to answered, bug fixed, needs a human), time from ticket to verified fix, refusals by reason, and drafts older than 48 hours with no human decision.

principles.title: Model the business as a line, and make the product predictable for the customer
principles.voice: Everyone wants a viral product. We build predictability, and buyers purchase predictability, not virality.
principles.why: The revenue model that compounded was 1.7× high within 26 days. The one that held is a line: flat intake times a retention plateau is a constant increment, so the planning number is the ceiling (adds per week divided by churn), never a far-off month. Predictability for the customer is the same discipline turned outward: anything they must be able to rely on becomes deterministic code, with the model as the fallback.

moves.text: Model the base as intake × retention plateau, not compounding. Quote the ceiling and the weekly add rate; state what has to stay true for a projection to land.
Name the lever: when the funnel is improving and intake is flat, the lever is intake, not conversion.
Backtest every projection against its own actuals on a dated schedule; replace the weakest assumption with a measured interval as soon as the sample exists.
Learn what people believe the product is from what they type and when they return, and align copy, prompts and pricing to that belief.
For anything the customer must be able to predict (formats, dates, prices, record writes), recognize the intent in code before any model runs; use the model for the remainder.
Build the outward-facing moat (what your users' own customers see) rather than matching the incumbent's back-office polish.

evidence.text: Linear fit R² 0.998 vs exponential 0.548 on paying accounts; the base grew 54% while paid adds sat flat at ~25 a week (R² 0.03). Ceiling ≈ $7,000 a month at those adds and 13% churn.
Churn assumed at 7% and measured at 13% (CI 8–20%); the far-month cell had been 1.7× too high and its caveat had hidden itself.

A user asked ten times for a formatting preference; it was stored twice and injected every turn, and the model ignored it in a third of outputs. A deterministic rewrite on finished text held: 45 of 74 real messages corrected, zero collateral.

Pricing questions answered from a matcher with zero model calls (from ~10 seconds); record writes parsed deterministically (~1.7s, no silent drops) instead of extracted by a model (6–11s, 3 of 6 dropped).

donts: Put a far-month cell in a revenue column that implies 5× today's acquisition with nothing scheduled to cause it.
Steer on the free base (“a distraction”) instead of paid adds.
Fix a probabilistic component (a model, a ranking, a recommendation) by asking it harder; “the fix that has already been tried, twice.”
principles.how_to_measure: Paid adds per week with a trend fit, churn on exposure with an interval, the implied ceiling, and a dated backtest calendar. For the product: the share of user-set preferences honored on output, measured by replaying real inputs; anything that must be reliable is code.

laws.law: Define “active” by a real product action and show it beside the flattering definition so inflation cannot silently return.
laws.incident: A click event fired for 1,482 of 1,487 users.

laws.law: One canonical internal-account filter, applied in every counter and both data layers, including browsers.
laws.incident: A teammate's test checkout was the paid suite's only customer.

laws.law: Aggregate in the database; a script acting on a population refuses to run when its count and the database's disagree.
laws.incident: A campaign audience came out as 101 of 3,015.

laws.law: Name events by behavior and surface, pin single emitters, and always record the impression so conversion has a denominator.
laws.incident: A preloaded form told 178 people they had started entering a card.

laws.law: Persist the system's own decisions beside its output so failures can be counted rather than reconstructed.
laws.incident: Nothing stored the granted budget, so severed answers could only be inferred from lengths.

laws.law: Reset reporting windows to instrumentation-complete instants, use named timezones, and flag reconstructed data forever.
laws.incident: A daylight-saving offset moved a funnel boundary.

laws.law: Blended engagement rates decay mechanically as a base ages; read cohorts by tenure.
laws.incident: The blend fell ~0.5–0.7 points per ten days with zero product change.

laws.law: Low-volume rates are noise dressed as signal below a month; fix one window and never shop for another.
laws.incident: Trailing-7 and calendar weeks told opposite stories.

laws.law: Build funnels per identity, per step, and refuse small-n precision.
laws.incident: “62.5% of eight people is false precision.”

laws.law: Derive revenue metrics from payment facts recorded when they occur, never from status strings, event names or reconstruction.
laws.incident: Only 6 of 20 “cancelled” accounts had ever paid.

laws.law: Any retention or email effect claim needs a recorded control group; never cite the treated group's coincidence rate.
laws.incident: Lifecycle email success rates were ~5× inflated.

laws.law: An experiment picker must distinguish missing instrumentation from a true zero.
laws.incident: 9,110 sends went out under the wrong subject.

laws.law: Flat intake times a plateaued retention curve is a constant increment; steer by add rate and ceiling, never the far cell.
laws.incident: Compounding inflated the far month 2.5× against the linear default case.

laws.law: Replace planning assumptions with measured intervals as soon as the sample exists, on a dated schedule.
laws.incident: 7% assumed, 13% measured.

laws.law: Silent-failure classes need scheduled read-only canaries with backtested thresholds that always emit a report.
laws.incident: Ten days of severed output produced zero tickets.
